summary: Collects several example applications that need authorization decisions, to help ground the design of authorization protocols. It is an informational companion to the other AAA authorization documents.

eli5.summary: This is a set of real-life stories about who gets to do what on a network, used to help designers decide what rules they need.

subtitle: Real-world authorization needs from dial-up, mobile, printing, e-commerce, and education services.

tldr.problem: Authorization protocols must support many different Internet applications, each with different authorization requirements. Without studying real use cases, a general protocol risks missing critical needs.
tldr.mechanism: The document presents detailed authorization scenarios from six important applications—dial-up roaming, mobile IP, bandwidth allocation, printing, electronic commerce, and distance learning—showing how each one handles who gets to do what.
tldr.outcome: These examples ground the design of authorization protocols and motivate a separate set of general authorization requirements that any AAA protocol must meet.

facts.label: Applications covered
facts.value: 6 detailed (dial-up, mobile IP, bandwidth broker, printing, e-commerce, education)

today: RFC 2905 is an Informational document providing historical context for AAA authorization design. The applications described—dial-up roaming, mobile IP, resource allocation, and multi-domain access—remain important to Internet infrastructure. The authorization patterns identified here have influenced the design of numerous access control systems and continue to inform authorization protocol work.

sections.title: Why Application Examples Matter
sections.content:
This document is one of three in a series on AAA (Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting) authorization architecture from the IETF Authorization Research Group. Rather than starting with protocol mechanics, the group decided to study real applications first—to ground protocol design in actual requirements.

For each application, the document presents a model of how authorization works, maps that model to an authorization framework, and lists what authorization features the application needs. These are not definitive specifications from the applications' own working groups, but rather starting points for understanding what protocols must support. The document includes five detailed applications and brief coverage of others, showing the breadth of authorization needs across the Internet.
sections.eli5: Before designing how to say "yes" or "no" to Internet requests, the authors looked at what different services actually need to allow and block.

sections.title: Dial-Up Roaming and Mobile IP
sections.content:
PPP dial-in with roaming covers users who travel and need to dial into different Internet service providers. When a user dials into a visited ISP, the visited ISP's AAA server forwards authentication to the user's home ISP, which makes the authorization decision. The home ISP returns service parameters (like idle timeout) to the visited ISP's network access server. This requires AAA protocols to forward requests between domains and support roaming brokers that add their own local information without breaking security.

Mobile IP extends this to wireless mobile devices moving across networks. The protocol must support security associations between multiple parties (mobile node, foreign agent, home agent), dynamic assignment of home agents and addresses, and minimal latency (ideally a single round trip). Mobile-IP AAA requirements include broker support with end-to-end security, resource management to track where nodes are, key distribution acting as a Key Distribution Center, and ability to send unsolicited messages to AAA clients.
sections.eli5: When you dial from another city, the local provider asks your home provider if it's okay. Mobile phones have similar needs—they move around and each place needs to talk to where you came from.

sections.title: Bandwidth Brokers and Resource Allocation
sections.content:
Bandwidth Broker authorization manages who gets what portion of network bandwidth for what quality of service. The model involves service users requesting resource allocation between specific source and destination addresses, with authorization based on contractual relationships between users and service providers.

In multi-domain scenarios, bandwidth brokers in different autonomous networks have contracts with each other. Trust relationships can be established through certificates, authentication methods, secure channels, or physical wiring knowledge (knowing which port connects to which user). Authorization decisions may involve brokers forwarding requests to other brokers, each adding their own local policy constraints. The authorization response includes QoS profiles describing the service parameters the user receives.
sections.eli5: Networks have a certain amount of fast data flow they can offer. Authorization decides which customers get how much and what quality they get.

sections.title: Internet Printing, E-Commerce, and Education
sections.content:
Internet Printing Protocol authorization determines who can submit jobs, set printer options, and retrieve results. It uses trust relationships including attribute certificates to grant permissions based on roles and group membership rather than just user identity.

Electronic commerce authorization spans both static trust relationships (like certificate authorities) and dynamic ones (like a payment gateway checking credit limits in real time). Authorization must work across multiple domains where different parties—customer, merchant, payment processor, shipper—have separate trust relationships. Pre-paid scenarios require authorization information issued long before a purchase decision.

Computer-based education and distance learning systems grant access to courses based on enrollment, prerequisite completion, and time-based rules. Users might be students, teachers, or administrators with different rights. Authorization must support sequences of requests where each decision depends on earlier actions, and integrate with both authentication and accounting to track usage and billing.
sections.eli5: Printing, shopping, and online schools all need to know whether someone should be allowed to do something, but what they need to check is different in each case.

sections.title: Common Themes Across Applications
sections.content:
Across all these applications, several authorization requirements emerge. Protocols must transport information about the requestor, the service requested, and the operating environment. They must support proxying—where one entity requests something on behalf of another. They must work across domain boundaries with appropriate security. Roaming must be possible, meaning a user from one domain can be served by another domain.

Authorization must be separable from authentication (sometimes you know who someone is, but need someone else to decide what they can do). Multiple services or applications must be authorized in a single exchange. Trust relationships must be configurable—an AAA entity might trust another entity for some purposes but not others. Session-based authorization must be possible, where authorization decisions change during an ongoing session.
sections.eli5: All these services need similar building blocks: knowing who's asking, what they want, whether different networks can work together, and whether rules can change while something is happening.

sections.title: Generalizing from Specific Applications
sections.content:
The examples in this RFC are not meant to be prescriptive for how applications should work. Rather, they illustrate patterns and extract requirements that any general-purpose authorization protocol should support. The requirements presented here were collected, generalized, and formalized in a separate RFC (2906) that lists the abstract requirements an AAA protocol must meet.

By grounding protocol design in real applications rather than starting with blank assumptions, the authorization research group ensured that the requirements reflected genuine Internet needs. Each application brought unique constraints, and the common patterns visible across them define what an authorization protocol must do.
sections.eli5: Looking at real services shows what any permission system needs to handle. The lessons from these examples help designers build authorization systems that actually work for the Internet.
